title: An escape hatch to JavaScript, inside a SELECT
description: Embed the [QuickJS](https://bellard.org/quickjs/) JavaScript engine inside DuckDB so a `SELECT` can call out to JS for the cases SQL doesn't have a primitive for — modern [ECMAScript](https://tc39.es/ecma262/) syntax, scalar and table-valued forms, parameter passthrough. Reach for it when SQL alone can't express the transform; stay in SQL when it can.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: QuickJS adds a row-by-row JavaScript escape hatch to DuckDB. The shape of the problem is usually one of: text or JSON manipulation that exceeds what regex or [`json_*`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/loading_json.html) functions express cleanly, custom parsing or formatting, or a JS snippet you already have and don't want to port to SQL.

bulletPoints.label: Conditional JSON reshaping
bulletPoints.description: When the output shape depends on values inside the input JSON, `quickjs_eval` with a per-row arrow function is more readable — and often faster to write — than a tower of `CASE` over [`json_extract`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions).

bulletPoints.label: Text munging beyond regex
bulletPoints.description: Tokenizers, lightweight parsers, custom slug rules, normalization passes that depend on imperative control flow. JS gives you `for`, `if`, `switch`, and string methods without leaving SQL.

bulletPoints.label: Array fan-out
bulletPoints.description: The table form of `quickjs` lets a JS expression return an array and have DuckDB emit one row per element — handy for unrolling computed sequences or splitting a value into its components.

bulletPoints.label: Reusing existing JS
bulletPoints.description: Validation rules, formatting helpers, or small library snippets you already trust in JavaScript can be dropped into a query without rewriting them.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: The extension links [QuickJS-NG](https://github.com/quickjs-ng/quickjs) — an actively-maintained fork of [Fabrice Bellard's QuickJS](https://bellard.org/quickjs/) — into DuckDB as scalar and table functions. Each call instantiates a JS context, evaluates the supplied source, and converts the result back across the SQL boundary. There is no shared state between rows.

bulletPoints.label: Two surfaces, picked by call site
bulletPoints.description: `quickjs` used after `SELECT` evaluates an expression and returns a `VARCHAR`. The same name used after `FROM` expects an array and unpacks it into rows. `quickjs_eval` calls a JS function with positional arguments and returns `JSON`.

bulletPoints.label: Argument binding
bulletPoints.description: Positional arguments to the table form of `quickjs` are exposed inside the JS as `arg0`, `arg1`, … . When an argument is a JSON-shaped string, a parsed copy is also bound as `parsed_arg0`, `parsed_arg1`, … so you don't pay for `JSON.parse` in the snippet.

bulletPoints.label: Modern ECMAScript
bulletPoints.description: QuickJS-NG implements the bulk of the [ECMAScript](https://tc39.es/ecma262/) standard — arrow functions, destructuring, `let`/`const`, `Map`/`Set`, `Promise`, modern `Array` / `String` / `Object` methods. No browser, no Node APIs (no `fetch`, `fs`, etc.) — this is a pure language runtime.

bulletPoints.label: Per-row evaluation
bulletPoints.description: Snippets are JIT-compiled within the QuickJS context per call. There's no cross-row caching of compiled functions, so cost scales linearly with input row count.

sections.title: When to reach for it (and when to stay in SQL)
sections.description: Row-by-row JavaScript is inherently slower than vectorized SQL. QuickJS is a power feature, not a default — use it when the expressiveness of JS justifies the cost.

bulletPoints.label: Prefer native DuckDB functions
bulletPoints.description: If [DuckDB's scalar functions](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/overview), [`json_*`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/loading_json.html) family, or [regex functions](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/patternmatching) cover your transform, they will be substantially faster — they run vectorized over column batches instead of one row at a time.

bulletPoints.label: Hot OLAP paths are the wrong place
bulletPoints.description: Per-row JS interpretation is fine for ETL and ad-hoc work over millions of rows. It is not the right tool for an interactive dashboard query that runs against a billion-row fact table on every refresh.

bulletPoints.label: Untrusted input is risky
bulletPoints.description: QuickJS is a sandbox in the sense that it has no I/O surface. It is not hardened against adversarial JS — don't `quickjs_eval` user-supplied source in a multi-tenant context.

bulletPoints.label: Consider Rhai for tighter SQL integration
bulletPoints.description: [`evalexpr_rhai`](/products/extensions/evalexpr_rhai) embeds the [Rhai](https://rhai.rs/) scripting language. Rhai is more constrained as a language, but it tends to integrate more cleanly with SQL types — fewer JSON round-trips at the boundary. Worth comparing if your snippet is small and type-driven.

useCases.title: Reshape semi-structured payloads
useCases.description: Per-row `quickjs_eval` with a small arrow function over a JSON column — readable when the output shape branches on values in the input.

useCases.title: Custom string transforms
useCases.description: Slug rules, identifier normalization, lightweight tokenization where regex stops being expressive enough.

useCases.title: Array fan-out from a computed expression
useCases.description: The table form of `quickjs` — generate a sequence in JS and let DuckDB emit one row per element — useful for unrolling permutations or test data.

useCases.title: Drop in an existing JS helper
useCases.description: Validation logic, date/string formatters, or small library snippets reused inside a SQL pipeline without porting them.
